title: Italianate style walk
premise: Round-headed fenestration, bracketed cornices and elevated stoops: five Italianate residences from 1612 to 2031 Prairie, representing the avenue's earliest architectural generation.

opening.text:
JAUNT: ITALIANATE STYLE. An autumn morning, 1904. Before the mansards and the granite, Prairie Avenue was constructed in the Italianate idiom: residences costumed as villas on a Tuscan hillside, the prevailing fashion of the 1860s, when the first substantial houses appeared along this avenue.

Identify three characteristic features: tall round-headed windows, deep cornices supported on carved brackets, and elevated stoops lifting the principal entrance above the street. Five residences on foot, from 1612 to 2031 Prairie, all belonging to the avenue's original generation.

Commence at 1612, with the most accomplished Italianate façade on the avenue.

stops.text: 1612 Prairie, Joseph Goodman's residence of 1869, constructed two years before the Great Fire. Its photograph documents the Italianate formula realized in stone: three bays, every window round-headed beneath an elongated keystone, a belt course articulating the principal floor, and an arched portico on columns surmounting an elevated stoop. The stoop is fundamental to the composition: a visitor ascends considerably above the street, and above the dust of its traffic, before the door opens, a spatial expression of social distance. The residence will survive until its demolition around 1960. Walk one block south, where the identical year's style acquires a celebrated architect.

1701 Prairie, William G. Hibbard's residence, likewise from 1869, designed by William Le Baron Jenney for the president of a substantial wholesale hardware enterprise. The district register classifies it as Italianate: a low hipped roof on bracketed eaves surmounting a stone-based body, with a rear range appended in 1874. Jenney would subsequently engineer the first skyscraper, an irony for an architect who began with domestic villas; this residence will be demolished in 1932. Two doors south stands something considerably rarer on this avenue: an Italianate residence constructed of timber.

1720 Prairie, the Tyrrell and Walker residence, which the district register identifies as an Italianate building of timber: a low hip on deep bracketed eaves, a central gable, a canted bay and a porch spanning the entire façade. The brick and stone fronts surrounding it demonstrate the direction the avenue ultimately pursued. In 1910 wreckers will make it the first of numerous Prairie Avenue residences demolished, as domestic architecture yields to offices, warehouses and factories. Compare its timber brackets with the masonry examples nearby. Cross Eighteenth Street to a residence that revised its appearance.

1834 Prairie, Fernando Jones's residence, designed by John M. Van Osdel and constructed in 1866 for "one of Chicago's earliest pioneers - Fernando Jones". It was originally Italianate. Two decades later the entire avenue had embraced the mansard, so in 1886 Jones appended a mansard addition "to bring it into fashion with many of its neighbors". Here, therefore, is an Italianate residence wearing a more fashionable hat, retained until its demolition in 1942. Prairie Avenue was an intensely competitive environment, where architectural currency signified social standing. One concluding stop lies beyond Twentieth.

2031 Prairie, the northern residence of a row of three constructed in 1869 with pale Lemont limestone façades. The district register classifies it as Italianate: a flat roof concealed behind a bracketed cornice, surmounting three stories. The three residences share a continuous cornice line, simulating a single unified palazzo, although each preserves an independent entrance. Identify where the brackets interrupt and recommence.

legs.story: Across Eighteenth Street, along the western sidewalk.

endings.text:
The Italianate walk concludes here. Count the brackets you encountered: these constitute the avenue's oldest façades, constructed before the fire and before the extraordinary fortunes that succeeded it.

By 1904 they already appear antiquated beside the mansards and the granite. Walk the Second Empire or Romanesque routes to examine what followed.

keepsake.title: Italianate field note
keepsake.text: A modern field note documenting the style's brackets and round-headed windows; not a period document.

evidence.text: Joseph Goodman Residence. Built 1869; architect unknown.
evidence.locator: The 1612 S. Prairie Avenue entry's name line.

evidence.text: The photograph shows a three-bay stone front, every window round-headed under voussoirs with a long keystone, a belt course at the principal floor, and an arched portico on columns at the head of a high stoop.
evidence.locator: The whole print: the stone street front from its south corner to its north corner, the stoop and the portico.

evidence.text: The front is read as Italianate.
evidence.reasoning: Round-headed windows under keystoned voussoirs, a belt course and an arched portico on a high stoop are the Italianate vocabulary of an 1869 stone front; the T-1837 register files the house Italianate stone-front masonry.

evidence.text: The district draft reads the Hibbard house from the T-1837 register as an Italianate mansion with a rear addition: a low hip on bracketed eaves over a stone-based body, and the 1874 rear range.
William G. Hibbard Residence. Built 1869; William Le Baron Jenney, architect; Hibbard was president of a large wholesale hardware firm (read in paraphrase).
evidence.locator: The 1701 S. Prairie Avenue entry: its name line, and its description as read in paraphrase.

evidence.text: Fernando Jones Residence. Built 1866; John M. Van Osdel, architect. In 1886, the Italianate residence received a mansard addition to bring it into fashion with many of its neighbors.

The district draft reads 2031 Prairie as the north house of an 1869 Lemont-limestone row: an Italianate flat roof behind a bracketed cornice over three storeys; the row shares one cornice line, and its doors differ.
The route, its order, its autumn morning, its reading times, its keepsake and its framing are modern interpretation; no historical visit, conversation or occupant on a day in 1904 is asserted.
The district draft reads the Tyrrell/Walker house from the T-1837 register as an Italianate frame house: a low hip on deep bracketed eaves, with a central gable, a canted bay and a full-width porch.
Van Osdel designed two houses on Prairie Avenue; 'The first of these, at 1834 S. Prairie Avenue, was built in 1866 for one of Chicago's earliest pioneers - Fernando Jones'.
Joseph Goodman Residence, 1612 S. Prairie Avenue: razed circa 1960.

William G. Hibbard Residence, 1701 S. Prairie Avenue: in 1921 the house was bought by the American Terra Cotta & Ceramic Co., which gave the architect Louis Sullivan free office space there until his death in 1924. Razed 1932.
In 1910 wreckers destroyed the mansion at 1720 Prairie, the first of many Prairie Avenue homes to be torn down, as the street's residences increasingly gave way to offices, warehouses and factories.
evidence.locator: The essay's closing paragraphs on the street's decline.

evidence.text: Fernando Jones Residence, 1834 S. Prairie Avenue: razed 1942.
